title: tsdk type bridges: Zod + JSON-Schema adapters for discriminated structured output
creator: Asha Patel
description:
Summary: Implement a TypeScript SDK codegen and runtime adapters that produce both TypeScript types and consumable Zod / JSON-Schema artifacts to reliably parse discriminated unions and streamed structured outputs. The goal is to give app teams first-class ergonomics for structured output (sync + streaming), reduce runtime parsing errors, and make it easy to validate/fallback when models drift.

Background: Current tsdk consumers hand-write ad-hoc parsers for structured output or rely on brittle string parsing. We already have several conversations and experimental helpers but lack a consolidated codegen + runtime strategy that: (1) generates TypeScript types, (2) emits Zod schemas or JSON-Schema for runtime validation, and (3) exposes streaming-safe adapters that can incrementally validate partial fragments and reconstruct discriminated unions.

Scope & Deliverables:
- Codegen CLI additions (tsdk-codegen) that, given a schema spec, emits: .d.ts (types), .zod.ts (zod schema + helpers), and .jsonschema.json. Output should follow a namespaced naming convention (ModelX.ts / ModelX.zod.ts).
- Runtime helpers inside @redwood/tsdk-runtime: safeParse(obj, schema), streamParse(stream, schema, options), createDiscriminatorGuard(discriminatorKey) and patching utilities for KV/prefix cache integration.
- Discriminator pattern: default to configurable key `__type` but allow user override. Codegen will synthesize a union type with a discriminant and produce a Zod.discriminatedUnion or fallback to Zod.union + custom refine for older zod versions.
- Streaming ergonomics: introduce a chunk envelope shape {event: 'chunk'|'done'|'error', type?: string, payload: any}. streamParse will accept partial payloads and call user-provided onFragment callbacks with validated partial data; it will attempt to merge fragments by discriminator when possible and emit final validated object on done.
- Example apps and recipes: chat structured output example, reranker with typed outputs, and migration guide for teams moving from ad-hoc parsing.

Technical decisions & trade-offs:
- Zod vs JSON-Schema: Zod is primary for runtime ergonomics in TS apps; we emit JSON-Schema as a secondary artifact for cross-language interop (Python/Go). Codegen will favor Zod when target is tsdk. JSON-Schema generation will be lossy for some Zod features and documented.
- Discriminated unions: Use discriminatedUnion API when all members share a single string literal field; otherwise generate a runtime 'type' resolver function. This avoids brittle heuristics but requires codegen to annotate unions.
- Streaming validation: Strict incremental validation can be expensive. We'll validate per-fragment using shallow schemas and perform full validation on final merge. Offer an option `strictStreamValidation: true|false` in runtime options. Default is false for latency-sensitive paths.
- Backwards compatibility: Expose helpers as opt-in packages: @redwood/tsdk-codegen (CLI) and @redwood/tsdk-structured (runtime). Existing codepaths remain unaffected unless teams opt-in.

Implementation plan (high level):
1) Prototype (1 week): minimal codegen that outputs types + zod for a small set of schemas; build streamParse prototype. Link: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/DEV/tsdk-structured-output-prototype
2) Codegen & runtime (2 weeks): full emitters, discriminator guards, and API surface. PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/tsdk/pull/2107
3) Examples & docs (3 days): three example repos and README recipes.
4) Integration tests & e2e (4 days): streaming e2e with simulated partial outputs; load test for stream validation latency. PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/infra/pull/582

Acceptance criteria:
- tsdk-codegen can emit TypeScript type + Zod schema for a provided spec file and builds without error.
- Runtime provides streamParse that can reassemble two-part fragment + pass full Zod validation.
- Example chat app demonstrates discriminated union with at least 3 variants in the SDK examples repo.
- Migration doc and quickstart exist in docs/tsdk/structured-output.md.

Risks & mitigations:
- Performance overhead: measure CPU/time for zod validation under high qps, provide opt-out flags and shallow validation mode.
- Schema drift: include telemetry (opt-in) to track validation failures and provide regression alerting in Redwood Console.
- Developer friction: provide CLI generator in monorepo and VSCode snippets to reduce uptake friction.

Next steps (short):
- Finalize discriminator key API (default to `__type`) and post on #tsdk-engineering for feedback.
- Kick off prototype branch and demo by 2026-03-08.

Example usage (pseudo-code):
```ts
// generated: User.zod.ts
export const UserZ = z.object({ __type: z.literal('user'), id: z.string(), name: z.string() });
export type User = z.infer<typeof UserZ>;

// runtime usage
import { streamParse, createDiscriminatorGuard } from '@redwood/tsdk-structured';
const guard = createDiscriminatorGuard('__type');
await streamParse(responseStream, UserZ, {
  onFragment: (frag) => { if (guard(frag)) console.log('partial user fragment', frag) },
  strictStreamValidation: false
});
```

streamParse merges fragments and validates final output with Zod
Docs + example app created and linked
Tests demonstrating strict and shallow validation modes
